candidate.answerReason: Both conditions require prime squares. The only primes p < q satisfying q² − p² = 48 are p = 11 and q = 13, giving n = 121. Exactly one integer works, matching choice B.

methods.label: Factor the difference of prime squares
methods.explanation:
We must have \(n>1\), since \(P(1)\) is undefined. For any integer \(m>1\), the condition \(P(m)=\sqrt m\) holds exactly when \(m\) is the square of a prime: if \(p=P(m)=\sqrt m\), then \(m=p^2\); conversely, the only prime factor of \(p^2\) is \(p\).

Therefore write \(n=p^2\) and \(n+48=q^2\), where \(p<q\) are primes. Factoring their difference gives
\[
(q-p)(q+p)=48.
\]
Set \(a=q-p\) and \(b=q+p\). These are positive integers with \(a<b\). They have the same parity because \(b-a=2p\). Since their product is even, they must both be even.

The smaller factor is at most \(6\), because \(7^2>48\). Thus the possible even factor pairs are exactly
\[
(a,b)=(2,24),\ (4,12),\ (6,8).
\]
Using \(p=(b-a)/2\) and \(q=(a+b)/2\), these give, respectively,
\[
(p,q)=(11,13),\ (4,8),\ (1,7).
\]
Only the first pair consists of two primes. It gives \(n=11^2=121\) and \(n+48=169=13^2\), which satisfy both original conditions. Every possible factor pair was considered, and each determines just one \(n\). Hence exactly \(\boxed{1}\) integer works, choice \(\text{B}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses prime meaning, difference-of-squares factoring, parity, and a complete list of small factor pairs.

methods.label: Bound the smaller prime and test the possibilities
methods.explanation:
The expression \(P(n)\) requires \(n>1\). Since a greatest prime factor is prime, \(P(m)=\sqrt m\) forces \(m\) to be a prime square. Conversely, every prime square has this property. Thus we seek primes \(p<q\) such that
\[
n=p^2,\qquad n+48=q^2.
\]
If \(p=2\), then \(q^2=52\), which lies strictly between \(7^2=49\) and \(8^2=64\), so this case is impossible.

Otherwise \(p\) is odd. Then \(q^2=p^2+48\) is odd, so \(q\) is also odd. Distinct odd integers differ by at least \(2\), giving \(q\ge p+2\). Consequently,
\[
48=q^2-p^2\ge(p+2)^2-p^2=4p+4,
\]
so \(p\le11\). The remaining prime possibilities are exactly \(3,5,7,11\).

For these values, \(q^2=p^2+48\) is respectively \(57,73,97,169\). The first three lie strictly between consecutive squares:
\[
49<57<64,\qquad64<73<81,\qquad81<97<100.
\]
The last is \(169=13^2\), with \(13\) prime. Hence the sole valid value is \(n=121\). The bound includes every possible smaller prime, so the count is \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\text{B}\).
